courses.title: Open Source Contribution Basics: Git, GitHub & Pull Requests
courses.subtitle: Ship a real PR this month — not a lecture about one.
courses.description: A 3-week studio: official GitHub how-tos, two hands-on labs (GitHub Skills + First Contributions), then a real issue you can actually open a pull request for. Quizzes check the commands; assignments check that you did the work.

modules.title: Week 1: Do the GitHub flow yourself
modules.summary: Watch the 4-minute PR, then leave a public PR URL in the assignment.

lessons.title: What is GitHub? (official, 2 min)
lessons.description: GitHub’s own walkthrough of a repo: where the code lives, how a team shares it, and why the Pull requests tab exists.

lessons.title: Create a pull request in 4 minutes | GitHub for Beginners
lessons.description: Official screen-share: branch, commit, push, Compare & pull request, then write a title a reviewer can scan. Pause and do it on your account.

lessons.title: How to Find GitHub Repos to Contribute To
lessons.description: Use GitHub search, topics, and the good-first-issue label to find active projects instead of guessing.

lessons.title: How to Find Good First Issues in Open Source
lessons.description: Beginner-friendly labels, maintainer channels, and aggregators so you are not staring at a 1,700-issue backlog.

lessons.title: Git Cheat Sheet & PR Workflow Handbook
lessons.description: GitHub’s education cheat sheet: status, branch, commit, remotes, and the commands you will use on every PR. Keep it open during the lab.

lessons.title: Lab: Open your first pull request
lessons.description: Complete GitHub Skills, then land a practice PR on First Contributions. Paste the URLs — watching does not count.

assignment.brief: Do the work on GitHub, then write what you actually ran. Two labs: GitHub Skills ‘Introduction to GitHub’ (https://github.com/skills/introduction-to-github) and First Contributions (https://github.com/firstcontributions/first-contributions). Either merged or still open is fine.
assignment.deliverable: A public PR URL plus the commands you used.

fields.label: GitHub Skills repo or completion URL
fields.placeholder: https://github.com/YOUR-USER/introduction-to-github
fields.hint: Copy the exercise to your account, finish the four steps (branch, commit, PR, merge), then paste that repo URL.

fields.label: Your First Contributions (or Skills) pull request URL
fields.placeholder: https://github.com/firstcontributions/first-contributions/pull/…
fields.hint: Must be a pull request, not the repo homepage.

fields.label: What you changed, in one sentence
fields.placeholder: Added my name to Contributors.md on a branch called …
fields.hint: If you cannot name the file and the branch, you did not finish the lab.

fields.label: Commands you actually ran
fields.placeholder:
git clone …
git checkout -b …
git add …
git commit -m …
git push origin …
fields.hint: Paste the real sequence, including the one that failed and what you did next.

checklist: The PR URL opens in an incognito window.
You named a file and a branch, not ‘I followed the video’.
The command list includes clone or fork, a branch, commit, and push.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Git & Contribution Basics
lessons.description: Branching, issue linking, and how you actually find a first issue.

questions.prompt: Which command creates a new feature branch and switches to it in one step?

options.text: git branch fix/issue-10
git checkout -b fix/issue-10
git commit -m 'fix issue'
git push origin main

questions.explanation: `git checkout -b fix/issue-10` (or `git switch -c`) creates the branch and checks it out. `git branch` only creates it; you would still need to switch.

questions.prompt: In a pull request body, how do you link the work to GitHub issue 42 so the issue can close when the PR merges?

options.text: Write the issue number only: 42
Use a closing keyword: Fixes #42
Tag @github
Put the issue URL in a commit that never gets pushed

questions.explanation: `Fixes #42`, `Closes #42`, or `Resolves #42` links the PR to the issue and can auto-close it on merge.

questions.prompt: You want beginner issues in Python on GitHub. Which search is the most useful starting point?

options.text: stars:>100000 is:closed
language:python label:"good first issue" state:open
filename:password.txt
org:ghost

questions.explanation: Filter by language plus a newcomer label and open state. Huge starred + closed searches hide the work you can actually take.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that belongs in a first contribution.

options.text: Read README and CONTRIBUTING before writing code.
Work on a branch, not on upstream main.
Force-push to the project's main branch.
Comment on the issue before (or as) you start, if the project asks you to.

questions.explanation: Read the room, branch off main, talk to maintainers. Never force-push someone else's default branch.

modules.title: Week 2: Fix a conflict with your own hands
modules.summary: SSH, rebase vs merge, then the GitHub Skills conflict lab — not a 60-minute crash course.

lessons.title: GitHub for Beginners: SSH, PAT, conflicts, sync a fork
lessons.description: GitHub engineers screen-share the stuff that actually blocks first-timers: add an SSH key, mint a PAT, resolve a conflict in the PR UI, sync a fork, and review a diff.

lessons.title: Git Branches, Merge, and Rebase (do this in a throwaway repo)
lessons.description: Create two branches, collide on the same line, merge, then rebase your feature onto updated main. Pause and reproduce each command locally.

lessons.title: GitHub Git Cheat Sheet
lessons.description: Keep this open while you resolve conflicts: fetch, merge, rebase, stash, and log.

lessons.title: Lab: Resolve a merge conflict
lessons.description: Run GitHub Skills ‘Resolve merge conflicts’, then write what the markers meant and what you kept.

assignment.brief: Start the official lab: https://github.com/skills/resolve-merge-conflicts (about 30 minutes). You can also manufacture a conflict in a throwaway repo: two branches, same line, different words, then merge.
assignment.deliverable: Proof you resolved a conflict, plus the final file contents in your own words.

fields.label: Skills lab repo or the PR where you resolved the conflict
fields.placeholder: https://github.com/YOUR-USER/resolve-merge-conflicts or a PR URL
fields.hint: A repo or PR link a classmate could open.

fields.label: What you saw and what you kept
fields.placeholder: <<<<<<< HEAD had … / ======= / >>>>>>> feature had … I kept … because …
fields.hint: Quote the two sides. ‘I clicked resolve’ is not enough.

fields.label: On your next feature branch, rebase or merge — and why
fields.placeholder: I would rebase onto latest main before the PR because…
fields.hint: Rebase your unpushed solo branch. Do not rebase a shared main.

checklist: You linked a repo or PR, not a docs page.
You described both sides of the conflict, not only the winner.
You said when you would not rebase.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Conflicts & History
lessons.description: Conflict markers, rebase vs merge, and what not to rewrite.

questions.prompt: You open a file after a failed merge and see <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. What should you do?

options.text: Commit immediately; Git already picked a winner.
Edit the file to the intended result, delete the markers, then add and commit.
Delete the repository and clone again.
Run git push --force on main.

questions.explanation: Conflict markers are a pause, not a result. You choose the code, remove the markers, then stage and commit the resolution.

questions.prompt: When is `git rebase` a reasonable tool on your own feature branch?

options.text: To replay your commits on top of latest main before you open a PR.
To rewrite commits already on the shared main branch.
To delete GitHub issues.
To skip code review.

questions.explanation: Rebase your unpushed (or solo) feature branch onto updated main. Do not rebase public history others already pulled.

questions.prompt: Select the true statements.

options.text: git fetch updates your remote-tracking branches without merging.
A merge commit records that two histories were joined.
git push --force on origin/main is standard for first-time contributors.
Small, focused commits are easier to review than one giant dump.

questions.explanation: Fetch is safe. Merge commits are a record. Force-pushing main is how you become unwelcome. Small diffs review faster.

modules.title: Week 3: Open a PR a maintainer can review
modules.summary: Pick a live issue, write the PR body, and draft the comment you will post.

lessons.title: Step-by-step: contribute to open source
lessons.description: Fork, clone, branch, commit, push, and open the PR — the full loop with the habits maintainers expect. Follow along on a real repo, not a notepad.

lessons.title: Studio: Claim a real issue and draft the PR
lessons.description: Find an open good-first-issue, extract the project’s rules, and write the PR description you would submit.

assignment.brief: Search `label:"good first issue" state:open` in a language you know. Read README + CONTRIBUTING. You do not have to merge this week — you do have to pick a real issue and write the artifacts a maintainer would read.
assignment.deliverable: Issue URL, three project rules, a PR body, and the issue comment you will post.

fields.label: Issue URL and why this one is sized for you
fields.placeholder: https://github.com/org/repo/issues/123 — it asks for … and the file to touch is …
fields.hint: Name the file or area. ‘It said good first issue’ is not a reason.

fields.label: Three rules from README / CONTRIBUTING you will follow
fields.placeholder:
1. Branch naming…
2. How to claim an issue…
3. Tests / DCO / PR template…
fields.hint: Quote the project, not generic Git advice.

fields.label: Draft PR title + body
fields.placeholder:
Title: Fix typo in …

## What
## Why
## How I tested
Fixes #123
fields.hint: Include a closing keyword if the issue should close on merge.

fields.label: The issue comment you will post
fields.placeholder: Hi — I’d like to take this. I will … Is this still open?
fields.hint: Short, specific, and ask if it is free. No ‘please assign me this thank you’ spam.

checklist: The issue URL is open on GitHub today.
The three rules came from that repo’s docs.
The PR body says what, why, how you tested, and Fixes #n.
The comment is something you would actually post.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Pull Requests
lessons.description: What a reviewable PR looks like.

questions.prompt: A reviewable first PR usually is:

options.text: A rewrite of the entire codebase.
Small, tested, and described, with the related issue linked.
Pushed straight to upstream main.
Opened without a description so reviewers 'see the code'.

questions.explanation: Maintainers merge small, explained changes. Giant surprise rewrites stall.

questions.prompt: CI on your PR is red. Best next move?

options.text: Ask for merge anyway; CI is optional.
Read the failing job, fix it on your branch, and push a follow-up commit.
Close the repo.
Open five more PRs to distract from it.

questions.explanation: Green checks are part of the contribution. Fix the branch; don't argue with the required workflow.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about review.

options.text: Review comments are normal; reply and/or push fixes.
You should discuss scope on the issue if the fix grows.
Changing files the issue never mentioned, silently, is a gift.
A polite, specific PR description saves a round of questions.

questions.explanation: Review is collaboration. Stay on scope unless you agree otherwise. Write like a teammate.

courses.title: GSoC, LFX & Outreachy: Mentorship Roadmap
courses.subtitle: Pick an org, draft the proposal, write the mentor note.
courses.description: Skip the ‘what is GSoC’ overview. This week you choose a program, shortlist issues, and write a proposal a mentor could mark up — using the official student guide plus accepted-proposal habits.

modules.title: Apply like a contributor, not a tourist
modules.summary: How people actually get in: org pick, contributions, proposal, mentor message.

lessons.title: How I got into GSoC: org pick, contributions, proposal
lessons.description: A contributor walkthrough: start on page two of the org list, write up your local setup as a first patch, stay on one org, and put a week-by-week timeline plus research in the proposal.

lessons.title: Nail your GSoC proposal (what mentors actually mark)
lessons.description: OpenMRS mentors on the template they use, the sections they skip, and why a messy draft sent early beats a perfect PDF at 23:59. Pair with https://google.github.io/gsocguides/student/writing-a-proposal

lessons.title: LFX Mentorship: how the board and terms work
lessons.description: Linux Foundation mentorships: terms, CNCF/kernel-adjacent projects, and how you apply on the LFX board (up to a few tailored projects per term).

lessons.title: Outreachy: initial application, then the contribution period
lessons.description: How the Outreachy initial application is structured and what the contribution period is for. Read the current applicant guide before you write: https://www.outreachy.org/docs/applicant/

lessons.title: Studio: Org shortlist + proposal draft
lessons.description: Pick one program and one org. List three issues. Write a 12-week proposal a mentor could comment on. Draft the first chat message.

assignment.brief: Use this year’s official pages — dates move. GSoC: https://summerofcode.withgoogle.com/ and the student proposal guide. LFX: https://mentorship.lfx.linuxfoundation.org/. Outreachy: https://www.outreachy.org/docs/applicant/. Depth on one org beats spraying twenty.
assignment.deliverable: A mentor-facing proposal draft, not an essay about your passion.

fields.label: Program + organization + why this pair
fields.placeholder: GSoC / LFX / Outreachy — org name — I can set this up locally because…
fields.hint: Name a language or repo you can compile this week. ‘Prestige org’ is not a reason.

fields.label: Three issues or idea-list items you would take first
fields.placeholder:
1. URL — what it asks — first file you would open
2. …
3. …
fields.hint: Real URLs. Include at least one you could finish before the application deadline.

fields.label: Proposal draft: problem, approach, 12-week timeline
fields.placeholder:
Problem the org has…
What I will ship (required vs optional)…
Weeks 1–4 / 5–8 / 9–12…
Risks and fallback…
fields.hint: Follow the official sections: https://google.github.io/gsocguides/student/writing-a-proposal — deliverables a mentor can check, not vibes.

fields.label: First message to a mentor (chat or email)
fields.placeholder: Hi — I built the project locally (blocked on X, fixed by Y). I read issue #… and I would start by … Does that match what you want?
fields.hint: Show setup + a specific issue. Do not send ‘please tell me how to start’ with no repo clone.

checklist: You named one program and one org, not five.
Every issue has a URL.
The timeline has weeks and deliverables, including a fallback.
The mentor note proves you ran the project locally.

lessons.title: Assessment: Mentorship Programs
lessons.description: Pick the right program — and the work that has to happen before the form.

questions.prompt: The strongest GSoC / LFX / Outreachy application usually includes:

options.text: Zero prior PRs and a very long essay.
Merged (or at least serious) contributions to the org, plus a specific proposal.
A promise to learn the language after selection only.
Copy-pasting last year's winning proposal unchanged.

questions.explanation: Mentors pick people they have already seen in the issue tracker. Proof of work beats a generic essay.

questions.prompt: Which pairing is most accurate?

options.text: Outreachy is only for people who already completed GSoC.
LFX Mentorship is run around Linux Foundation / CNCF-style projects in seasonal terms.
GSoC still requires you to be enrolled in a university.
All three programs merge your PRs without a mentor.

questions.explanation: LFX is the LF/CNCF mentorship board. GSoC has not required student status since 2022. Outreachy has its own eligibility (underrepresented in tech) and a contribution phase. Always read the current year's rules.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement.

options.text: Read this year's official timeline; dates move.
Pick 1–2 orgs and show up in their chat/issues early.
You can skip CONTRIBUTING.md if the stipend is large.
A proposal should name a project, a mentor-facing plan, and a realistic schedule.

questions.explanation: Timelines change. Depth beats spraying 20 orgs. Proposals are project plans, not vibes. Process docs still apply.

courses.title: Building Your Own Product: Idea to Launch
courses.subtitle: Four outcomes: submit an idea, talk to customers, ship a product, name the brand.
courses.description: The only builder studio in the library. You leave with four artifacts on this device: a locked idea, interview notes from a real person, a live product URL, and a brand plus first-user list. Other courses stay on Git and pitching — this one is the build.
outcomes: Idea submitted — one problem, one customer, locked for the month
Customers talked to — notes from a real conversation, not a survey
Product built — a live URL someone else can click
Brand named — a promise people can repeat, plus the first 20 users

modules.title: Week 1: Submit the idea
modules.summary: Lock one problem and one customer. Everything later in this course is about this idea.

lessons.title: How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas | Startup School
lessons.description: Jared Friedman’s questions you apply to a real idea this week: who already needs this, why you, why now. Pause after each question and write the answer you will submit.

lessons.title: Lean Canvas Template
lessons.description: Fill problem, customer, UVP, and channel before you write code. Empty boxes mean the idea is not submitted yet.

lessons.title: Outcome 1: Submit your idea
lessons.description: Hand in the idea you will build for the rest of this course. After this, changing the customer is a rewrite, not a tweak.

assignment.brief: Pick one problem a named person already has. This submission is the brief for weeks 2–4 — interviews, the product URL, and the brand all have to match it.
assignment.deliverable: A locked idea a classmate could explain back to you.

fields.label: The idea in one sentence
fields.placeholder: We help [who] do [job] without [pain].
fields.hint: Name the job, not the category. ‘It’s an AI platform’ is not an idea.

fields.label: The first customer (a real type of person, not ‘everyone’)
fields.placeholder: Second-year students who already… / shop owners on Instagram who…
fields.hint: If you cannot picture where they sit on a Tuesday, it is too wide.

fields.label: Why this is a real problem (something they already do or pay for)
fields.placeholder: They currently use WhatsApp + a notebook, and last week they…
fields.hint: Past behavior. ‘They would love this’ does not count.

fields.label: What you will not build this month
fields.placeholder: No mobile app / no payments / no admin / no second customer type…
fields.hint: If this list is empty, you have not submitted an idea — you have submitted a wishlist.

checklist: A stranger can say the one-liner back.
The customer is narrow enough to find this week.
You named something they already do, not a compliment they might give.
You cut work you will refuse.

lessons.title: Week 1 Assessment: Idea worth submitting
lessons.description: What makes an idea worth locking for a month.

questions.prompt: The strongest signal an idea is worth submitting is:

options.text: It sounds impressive when you pitch it at a party.
You (or people you can name) already feel this problem and already work around it.
No one has ever tried anything like it.
It requires the least possible work to build.

questions.explanation: Submit problems people already live with. Novelty and ease are not the test.

questions.prompt: A submitted idea should usually name:

options.text: Every feature on the year-one roadmap.
One customer, one job, and what you will not build yet.
A company name and a logo only.
A fundraising target.

questions.explanation: The submission is a constraint: who, what job, and the cuts.

questions.prompt: Select every section that belongs on a Lean Canvas before you build.

options.text: Problem
Unique Value Proposition
Office lease terms
Customer segment

questions.explanation: Problem, customer, UVP, channel, and metrics — not operations.

modules.title: Week 2: Talk to a customer
modules.summary: Run a Mom Test conversation about the idea you submitted. Notes beat opinions.

lessons.title: The Mom Test: how to talk to customers without lying to yourself
lessons.description: Rob Fitzpatrick on the three rules: talk about their life, ask about the last time (not ‘would you’), and listen more than you pitch. Pause and write the questions you will actually ask.

lessons.title: How To Talk To Users | Startup School
lessons.description: How to find people, book the call, and turn notes into a build/kill decision — without pitching first.

lessons.title: Outcome 2: Talk to a customer
lessons.description: Interview one real person about the idea you submitted. Write what they already do — not whether they like your pitch.

assignment.brief: Use the idea from week 1. Talk about their last week, not your solution. Best prompt: ‘Walk me through the last time this happened.’ A scheduled interview with a full script counts if you name the person and the time.
assignment.deliverable: Proof you talked to a customer: eight questions, notes, and a keep / kill / rewrite.

fields.label: Who you are interviewing and the last time they hit this problem
fields.placeholder: Name / role — last Tuesday they … and they used …
fields.hint: A real person. ‘Students in general’ is not an interview.

fields.label: Eight Mom Test questions you will ask
fields.placeholder:
1. Walk me through the last time…
2. What did you try?
3. What did that cost you?
…
fields.hint: Ban ‘Would you use this?’ and ‘Is this a good idea?’

fields.label: Interview notes (or the scheduled script if the call is this week)
fields.placeholder: They currently… They already paid for… They refused to… Commitment they offered…
fields.hint: Write behavior and commitments. Compliments do not count as signal.

fields.label: Keep / kill / rewrite the submitted idea — what changed
fields.placeholder: Decision: keep / kill / rewrite because they already… The one-liner is now …
fields.hint: If nothing about the idea moved, you pitched instead of interviewing.

checklist: You named a person, not a demographic.
None of the eight questions pitch the product.
Notes include something they already do or already pay for.
The keep / kill / rewrite names what you heard.

lessons.title: Week 2 Assessment: Talking to customers
lessons.description: Mom Test rules and what belongs on a Lean Canvas.

questions.prompt: Which question is most likely to pass the Mom Test?

options.text: Would you use an app that does this?
Walk me through the last time this problem showed up. What did you do?
Isn’t this a great idea?
On a scale of 1–10, how excited are you?

questions.explanation: Ask about a specific past episode and what they already did. Opinions and compliments are polite lies.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of an early user interview?

options.text: Convince the user your idea is good.
Understand their current behavior and pain points without pitching your solution.
Get them to pre-pay immediately.
Ask only yes/no questions to save time.

questions.explanation: Good interviews focus on understanding existing behavior and pain. Pitching too early biases the feedback you get.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that belongs in a customer conversation.

options.text: Ask about the last time the problem showed up.
Write down what they already do or already pay for.
Pitch the full product in the first two minutes.
End by asking for a small commitment (intro, follow-up, a try).

questions.explanation: Past behavior and a real next step beat a pitch. Compliments are not signal.

modules.title: Week 3: Build the product
modules.summary: Ship the smallest version of the submitted idea. The outcome is a URL, not a spec.

lessons.title: Michael Seibel — How to Plan an MVP
lessons.description: What actually counts as an MVP: the smallest thing that delivers value to a few users. Pause and delete features from your list as he talks.

lessons.title: Value Proposition Canvas (fill this, 5 min)
lessons.description: Alex Osterwalder’s official walkthrough: customer jobs, pains, gains vs your pain relievers and gain creators. If a box is empty, that feature is not in the MVP.

lessons.title: Outcome 3: Build the product (live URL)
lessons.description: Ship something a stranger can click: a site, form, bot, or demo. A spec without a URL does not count.

assignment.brief: Build the idea from week 1 using whatever is fastest — Carrd, Notion, Google Form, WhatsApp flow, Replit, Next.js. Ugly is fine. Private-only Figma is not a product.
assignment.deliverable: A live URL plus what it does and who already clicked it.

fields.label: Live product URL
fields.placeholder: https://… (or a public form / bot / demo link)
fields.hint: Must open without a login you cannot share. If it is a WhatsApp number or form, write the exact link or handle.

fields.label: What a user can do in 60 seconds
fields.placeholder: They land → they … → they get … That is the only job.
fields.hint: One job from the submitted idea. If you need a tutorial, it is too big.

fields.label: How you built it (tools + what you cut)
fields.placeholder: Built in … I skipped accounts / payments / mobile because…
fields.hint: Name the stack. Name the cuts. ‘I used AI’ is not a build log.

fields.label: Who already used it (name + what they did)
fields.placeholder: I sent it to [name]. They … They got stuck on … Next I will …
fields.hint: At least one real person. ‘I will share later’ fails the outcome.

checklist: The URL opens for someone who is not you.
The job matches the idea you submitted.
You named what you refused to build.
A named person already tried it.

lessons.title: Week 3 Assessment: Shipping an MVP
lessons.description: Scoping an MVP and problem–solution fit.

questions.prompt: Per Michael Seibel's MVP framework, what should your first MVP optimize for?

options.text: Supporting every feature you can imagine.
The smallest thing you can ship to test if you can deliver real value to a few users.
A polished, investor-ready product.
Building for a huge, general audience from day one.

questions.explanation: Seibel's advice: launch something ridiculously simple to a narrow set of early users first, then iterate on what you learn.

questions.prompt: On the Value Proposition Canvas, problem–solution fit means:

options.text: You listed as many features as the competitor.
Your pain relievers and gain creators match jobs, pains, and gains you observed.
You registered a domain.
Investors liked the deck.

questions.explanation: Fit is when the value map hits real jobs, pains, and gains — not when the feature list is long.

questions.prompt: Select every habit that matches 'launch something bad quickly' thinking.

options.text: Ship a limited version to a small set of users this week.
Delay launch until every edge case is handled.
Treat the first release as a way to learn, not a finished product.
Talk to the first users again after they try it.

questions.explanation: MVP thinking favors fast, narrow releases you learn from, not indefinite polishing before anyone sees it.

modules.title: Week 4: Build the brand and get first users
modules.summary: Name the promise, write the launch post, and put the live product in front of 20 people.

lessons.title: How to Get Your First Customers | Startup School
lessons.description: Gustaf Alströmer’s founder sales loop: make a list, send a short note, run a demo, track drop-off. Pause and start the spreadsheet of 20 names.

lessons.title: How to Launch on Product Hunt (Official Guide)
lessons.description: Product Hunt’s own walkthrough of preparing a hunter, a first comment, and a live URL — do this after friends already use the product.

lessons.title: Outcome 4: Brand + first 20 users
lessons.description: Write the brand promise for the product you shipped, then put that URL in front of 20 people.

assignment.brief: Brand is the sentence people repeat when you are not in the room. Pair it with the live URL from week 3 and a list of people you will actually message.
assignment.deliverable: A brand promise, a launch post with the product URL, and a named first-20 list.

fields.label: Brand promise (one sentence people can repeat)
fields.placeholder: For [who], we are the [category] that [unique outcome].
fields.hint: If it still works after you swap in a rival’s name, it is not a brand yet.

fields.label: The first 20 people or rooms who will see the live product
fields.placeholder:
Day 1–3: message these people…
Day 4–7: post in this room…
Link I will send: …
fields.hint: Names, groups, or shops. Include the product URL. ‘Go viral’ is not a plan.

fields.label: The short note you will send (paste-ready)
fields.placeholder: Hey [name] — I built X because you said Y. Can you try this URL this week and tell me if Z still hurts?
fields.hint: About their last problem, the live URL, one ask.

fields.label: Launch post — tagline, who it’s for, product URL
fields.placeholder:
Tagline: …
Who it’s for: …
Link: …
Maker comment: …
fields.hint: A stranger should know what to click. The link must be the thing you built.

checklist: The promise is specific enough to reject customers.
The 20-user plan names people or rooms and includes the live URL.
The note asks for a try, not a compliment.
The launch post has a tagline and the product link.

lessons.title: Week 4 Assessment: Brand & first users
lessons.description: Founder-led sales and launching as a repeatable process.

questions.prompt: For your first customers, Gustaf’s Startup School advice is to:

options.text: Buy ads before you can describe the buyer.
Make a list of the easiest likely buyers, message them yourself, and track each step of the funnel.
Wait until the product is famous.
Hire a salesperson in week one.

questions.explanation: First customers are founder-led and unscalable: a list, a note, a demo, and numbers on drop-off.

questions.prompt: Per Product Hunt's official launch guide, which practice most improves a launch?

options.text: Submitting with no prior engagement on the platform.
Participating in the community and building relationships before launch day.
Launching without a live product URL.
Avoiding all outside promotion.

questions.explanation: Product Hunt recommends genuine, sustained participation (comments, upvotes, feedback) well before your own launch, not a cold submission.

questions.prompt: Select every legitimate way to 'launch again' for an existing product.

options.text: Announcing a major new feature.
Re-launching to a new audience or platform.
Reposting the exact same launch post daily.
Sharing a milestone (users, revenue, an integration) as its own moment.

questions.explanation: Each real update, audience, or milestone is a legitimate reason to launch again — spamming the same post isn't.

courses.title: Entrepreneurship Studio: Brand, Product, Sales & Pitch
courses.subtitle: Write the company, the offer, the outreach, and the deck — this month.
courses.description: The founder voice — thesis, brand language, sales script, and a deck you can say out loud. The idea → customer → shipped-product loop lives only in Building Your Own Product.

modules.title: Week 1: Pick a problem you can sell this quarter
modules.summary: Stress-test the idea, then write the 90-day outcome and the first customer list.

lessons.title: How to Get and Evaluate Startup Ideas | Startup School
lessons.description: Jared Friedman’s questions you apply to a real idea this week: who already needs this, why you, why now. Pause after each question and answer it for your company.

lessons.title: How to Get Your First Customers | Startup School
lessons.description: The founder sales loop you will run in week 4: list, note, demo, close. Start the spreadsheet of names while you watch.

lessons.title: Assignment 1: Founder Thesis & 90-Day Outcome
lessons.description: Write the company in one sentence, why you are the person to build it, and one leadership outcome that will be true in 90 days.

assignment.brief: Pick a real problem you would spend a year on — not a class project. Leadership here means an observable outcome, not a vibe.
assignment.deliverable: A founder thesis you can say out loud without slides.

fields.label: The company in one sentence
fields.placeholder: We help [who] do [job] without [pain].
fields.hint: Lead with what you do. No adjectives that a competitor could copy-paste.

fields.label: Why you (founder-market fit)
fields.placeholder: I have lived this problem because…
fields.hint: Specific history beats 'I am passionate about this space.'

fields.label: Leadership outcome in 90 days
fields.placeholder: By day 90, these 10 people will…
fields.hint: Name a result a stranger could check: users, conversations, revenue, a shipped loop — not 'have a better culture.'

fields.label: What you will not do for 90 days
fields.placeholder: I will not hire a sales team / redesign the logo / …
fields.hint: Founders fail by adding work. List the tempting distractions you are cutting.

checklist: A stranger would understand what you do after the first sentence.
The 90-day outcome is observable, not motivational.
You named work you will refuse, not only work you will start.

modules.title: Week 2: Write the offer, then pick one channel
modules.summary: Fill a value proposition, then decide where you will show up weekly.

lessons.title: Value Proposition Canvas (fill this, 5 min)
lessons.description: Osterwalder’s official canvas: jobs, pains, gains vs pain relievers and gain creators. Fill it for your company before you write the brand promise.

lessons.title: PR + Content for Growth | Kat Mañalac & Craig Cannon
lessons.description: How founders actually sell a brand: owned content first, then press. Pause and pick the one platform you will post on this month.

lessons.title: Assignment 2: Brand Promise & Competitor Map
lessons.description: Write the brand promise, pick the first platform you will sell it on, and map three alternatives you refuse to look like.

assignment.brief: Brand is the sentence people repeat when you are not in the room. Competition is who they compare you to instead — including doing nothing.
assignment.deliverable: A one-page brand brief plus a three-player competitor map.

fields.label: Brand promise (one sentence people can repeat)
fields.placeholder: For [who], we are the [category] that [unique outcome].
fields.hint: If it works for a rival after a name swap, it is not a brand yet.

fields.label: Who it is for — and who it is not for
fields.placeholder: For: … / Not for: …
fields.hint: Narrow is a strategy. 'Everyone who wants to be productive' is not.

fields.label: Three alternatives and how you win
fields.placeholder: 1. Status quo / 2. Direct rival / 3. Adjacent tool — and why a user switches.
fields.hint: Include the status quo (doing nothing, Excel, a WhatsApp group). That is usually the real competitor.

fields.label: First platform you will sell the brand on
fields.placeholder: I will show up weekly on … because the buyers already gather there.
fields.hint: Pick one: a community, marketplace, newsletter, or social surface. 'Everywhere' is how brands stay invisible.

checklist: The promise is specific enough to reject customers.
At least one competitor is the status quo, not another startup logo.
You named one platform, not five.

modules.title: Week 3: Product people come back to + 20-user plan
modules.summary: Define the smallest lovable version, then name how 20 people try it.

lessons.title: How to Build Products Users Love | Kevin Hale
lessons.description: Support-driven product: make a few people unconditionally want you to succeed. Write down the support channel you will sit on this month.

lessons.title: Assignment 3: Product Promise & First-Channel Plan
lessons.description: Define the smallest lovable product, the first marketing channel, and how you will get 20 people to try it.

assignment.brief: Marketing cannot rescue a product nobody returns to. Write the product as a job, then pick one channel you will work this month.
assignment.deliverable: A product promise plus a first-channel plan for 20 users.

fields.label: Who + job-to-be-done + smallest lovable version
fields.placeholder: When [situation], [who] wants to [job], so they can [outcome]. The first version only does …
fields.hint: If the first version needs a roadmap to be useful, it is not first.

fields.label: What 'love' looks like in week one
fields.placeholder: They come back / they pay / they text a friend because…
fields.hint: Name a behavior, not a feeling. 'They said it was cool' does not count.

fields.label: First marketing channel and why it fits
fields.placeholder: I will use [channel] because my users already …
fields.hint: Match the channel to where the buyer already spends attention. Paid ads are rarely first.

fields.label: Plan to get the first 20 people to try it
fields.placeholder: Day 1–7: list, messages, places I will show up…
fields.hint: Do things that do not scale. Names, DMs, communities, office hours — not 'viral loop TBD.'

checklist: The first version is small enough to ship this month.
Love is a behavior you can count.
The 20-user plan names real places or people, not a funnel diagram.

modules.title: Week 4: Sales script, deck outline, send the note
modules.summary: Write the spoken pitch, the 10 slides, and one outbound note you would send today.

lessons.title: How to Sell | Tyler Bosmeny
lessons.description: Founders are the first salespeople: prospecting, a short personalized note, listening on the call, and asking for the close. Draft your note while he talks.

lessons.title: How to Pitch Your Seed-Stage Startup | Michael Seibel
lessons.description: A pitch is what you do, who is on the team, traction, insight, market, and the ask — said clearly enough that someone can fund or buy it. Template notes: https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/intro-to-the-yc-seed-deck

lessons.title: Assignment 4: Pitch Deck Outline & First Sales Script
lessons.description: Write the spoken pitch, the 10-slide deck outline, a cold note you would actually send, and where you will sell the brand this week.

assignment.brief: Sales and the deck are the same story told to different rooms. If you cannot say it in two sentences, the slides will not save you.
assignment.deliverable: A spoken pitch, a 10-slide outline, and one outbound note.

fields.label: Spoken pitch (what / who / why now / ask)
fields.placeholder: We do X for Y. The reason this works now is Z. We are asking for…
fields.hint: Two or three sentences a person could repeat after you leave the room.

fields.label: 10-slide pitch deck outline
fields.placeholder:
1. Purpose
2. Problem
3. Solution
4. Why now
5. Market
6. Competition
7. Model
8. Team
9. Traction / plan
10. Ask
fields.hint: One idea per slide. Write the title and the single sentence on the slide — not a paragraph of speaker notes. Use YC’s seed-deck order if you want a default.

fields.label: Cold note to a first customer or partner
fields.placeholder: Subject + 4–6 lines. Personalized. One ask: time this week.
fields.hint: Short, specific, and about them. The only job of this note is a conversation.

fields.label: Where you will sell the brand this week
fields.placeholder: This week I will post / message / show up on [platform] with [artifact].
fields.hint: Name the platform, the artifact (post, listing, thread, demo), and the person you want to reach.

checklist: The spoken pitch does not need a slide to make sense.
Each deck slide is one idea.
The cold note asks for time, not a purchase.
You named one platform and one artifact for this week.
